19. Then Ragā, the daughter of Māra, spoke this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
"Having cut off craving, the leader of a company and community <note>original: "gaṇa-saṅgha-vârî"; usually read gaṇasaṅghacārī, "one who moves at the head of a group and an order"</note>,
surely many beings too will follow his course¹ <note>the manuscripts marked SS. read "will cross over"</note>.
Alas, this homeless one <note>original: "anoko", "one without a house", that is, the Buddha</note> will snatch away
many people and lead them to the far shore, beyond the King of Death."
20. "The great heroes, the <term>Tathāgatas</term> <gloss>Thus-gone Ones, a title of the Buddhas</gloss>, lead indeed by the true Dhamma.
When those who understand are led by the Dhamma, what room is there for envy?"
21. Then Taṇhā, Arati and Ragā, the daughters of Māra, went to where Māra the Evil One was.
22. Māra the Evil One saw Taṇhā, Arati and Ragā, his daughters, coming from afar. Seeing them, he addressed them in verses:
"Fools! You tried to crush a mountain with lotus stalks,
to dig up a hill with your fingernails, to chew iron with your teeth.
As though you had lifted a rock upon your heads, you sought a footing in the bottomless abyss;
as though you had struck your breast against a stump, you come away from Gotama disheartened."
23. Glittering they had come, Taṇhā, Arati and Ragā;
the Teacher swept them away right there, as the wind sweeps off a fallen tuft of cotton.
<note>Taṇhā, Arati and Ragā are personifications: "Craving", "Discontent" and "Lust". Their failed attempt to seduce the Buddha closes the collection of discourses on Māra.</note>

In just the same way, great king, a monk drenches, steeps, fills and pervades this very body with a happiness free of rapture, so that there is no part of his whole body that is not suffused with that happiness free of rapture. <note>The printed form reads "tipatitakena", which appears to be a misreading of "nippītikena", "free of rapture", the standard phrase for the third absorption.</note>

This too, great king, is a fruit of the recluse's life visible here and now, more excellent and more sublime than the visible fruits of the recluse's life described before.

68. And further, great king, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the earlier disappearance of joy and sorrow, a monk enters and dwells in the fourth <term>jhāna</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss>, which is neither painful nor pleasant and has a purity of mindfulness born of equanimity. He sits pervading this very body with a pure, bright mind, so that there is no part of his whole body that is not suffused with that pure, bright mind.

Just as, great king, a man might sit wrapped from head to foot in a white cloth, so that there would be no part of his whole body not covered by the white cloth; in just the same way, great king, a monk sits pervading this very body with a pure, bright mind, so that there is no part of his whole body that is not suffused with that pure, bright mind.

This too, great king, is a fruit of the recluse's life visible here and now, more excellent and more sublime than the visible fruits of the recluse's life described before.

69. And further, great king, when his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, supple, workable, steady and attained to imperturbability, that monk directs and inclines his mind. <note>In the standard text the mind is directed "to knowledge and vision" (ñāṇadassanāya); that phrase does not appear in the printed text on this page.</note> He understands thus: "This body of mine has form; it is made of the four great elements, born of mother and father, built up out of rice and porridge, and is subject to impermanence, to rubbing and pressing, to breaking up and dispersal. And this consciousness <note>original: "viññāṇa"</note> of mine is supported here and bound up here."

70. Just as, great king, there might be a beautiful beryl gem <note>original: "maṇi veḷuriyo"</note> of the finest water, eight-faceted, well cut, clear, translucent, flawless, perfect in every respect, and through it a thread is strung, blue or yellow or red or white or brown. A man with good eyes, taking it in his hand, would examine it: "This is a beautiful beryl gem of the finest water, eight-faceted, well cut, clear, translucent, flawless, perfect in every respect; and through it a thread is strung, blue or yellow or red or white or brown."

<summary>King Ajātasattu is told of the further fruits of the recluse's life: the happiness of the third absorption and the pure, bright awareness of the fourth, each illustrated by a simile. The monk then turns his concentrated mind to insight, seeing the body as impermanent and consciousness as bound to it, illustrated by the simile of a thread seen through a clear beryl gem.</summary>

17. Or else, discontented, dissatisfied, wishing to fall away from the recluse's life, troubled by the training rule, ashamed of it, disgusted with it, longing for the household life, <term>pe</term> <gloss>and so on: the repeated passage is abbreviated in the text</gloss> longing to be no longer a son of the Sakyan <note>i.e. no longer a follower of the Buddha; the printed form is garbled here</note>, he says and declares: "I have a mother; she will support me." He says and declares: "I have a father; he will support me." He says and declares: "I have a brother; he will support me." He says and declares: "I have a sister; she will support me." He says and declares: "I have a son; he will support me." He says and declares: "I have a daughter; she will support me." He says and declares: "I have a wife; she will support me." He says and declares: "I have relatives; they will support me." He says and declares: "I have friends; they will support me." He says and declares: "I have a village; I will live by that." He says and declares: "I have a market town; I will live by that." He says and declares: "I have a field; I will live by that." He says and declares: "I have a house-site; I will live by that." He says and declares: "I have money; I will live by that." He says and declares: "I have gold; I will live by that." ... and so on ... He says and declares: "I have a craft; I will live by that." In this way too, monks, there is a declaration of weakness, but the training is not renounced. <note>original: "dubbalyāvikammañceva hoti sikkhā ca apaccakkhātā". A monk who merely voices his wish to return to lay life has shown weakness but has not formally given up the training, so he is still a monk and still bound by its rules.</note>

18. Or else, discontented, dissatisfied, wishing to fall away from the recluse's life, troubled by the training rule, ashamed of it, disgusted with it, longing for the household life, ... and so on ... longing to be no longer a son of the Sakyan, he says and declares: "It is hard." He says and declares: "It is not easy." He says and declares: "It is hard to practise." He says and declares: "It is not easy to practise." He says and declares: "I cannot make the effort." He says and declares: "I cannot endure it." He says and declares: "I take no pleasure in it." ... and so on ... He says and declares: "I take no delight in it." In this way too, monks, there is a declaration of weakness, but the training is not renounced.

19. And how, monks, is there a declaration of weakness and the training renounced? Here, monks, a monk who is discontented, dissatisfied, wishing to fall away from the recluse's life, troubled by the training rule, ashamed of it, disgusted with it, longing for the household life, ... and so on ... longing to be no longer a son of the Sakyan, says and declares: "I renounce the Buddha." In this way, monks, there is a declaration of weakness and the training is renounced. <note>Unlike the wishes and complaints above, an explicit statement of renunciation counts as formally leaving the order. A person who has done so is no longer a monk.</note>

<summary>This passage from the Vinaya's first rule of defeat lists the ways a dissatisfied monk may voice his wish to return to lay life: naming family, property or skills that could support him, or complaining that the holy life is hard. Such words show weakness but do not count as leaving the order; only an explicit statement such as "I renounce the Buddha" formally gives up the training.</summary>

Scholar Kong Xueli was a descendant of the Sage <note>Confucius, whose family name was Kong</note>. He was a man of refined and gentle bearing, and skilled at poetry. A close friend of his, the magistrate of Tiantai <note>a county in Zhejiang</note>, sent a letter inviting him to come. The scholar went, but the magistrate had just died. Stranded and penniless, unable to return home, he lodged at Putuo Temple, where the monks hired him to copy texts for them. A hundred-odd paces west of the temple stood the mansion of Mr. Shan. Mr. Shan was the son of a high-ranking family; a great lawsuit had brought him to ruin, and with few left in his household he had moved to live in the countryside, so the house stood empty. One day, as heavy snow whirled down and all was silent with not a traveller on the road, Kong happened to pass its gate. A young man came out, of very handsome and elegant appearance. Seeing the scholar, he hurried over to greet him with a bow, offered a few words of sympathy for his plight, and begged him to come inside. The scholar took a liking to him and gladly followed him in. The rooms were not very large, but brocade curtains hung everywhere, and on the walls were many works of calligraphy and painting by old masters. instead of using boards or rods, he just stood there and beat him with whatever he could lay his hands on, and broke the skin on his face in two places. We heard that you have some kind of medicine here, Aunt Xue, for wounds from a beating with the rod; Miss, would you find a pill for me?"

When Baochai heard this, she at once told Ying'er to find two pills and give them to Ping'er. "In that case," Baochai said, "give him my regards. I won't go myself." Ping'er assented to Baochai and left. Of this no more need be said.

Now Xiangling, after she had greeted everyone and had supper, when Baochai and the others had all gone to Grandmother Jia's, went by herself to the Xiaoxiang Lodge. <note>The Xiaoxiang Lodge, "Bamboo Lodge," is Lin Daiyu's residence in the Grand View Garden.</note> By now Daiyu was mostly recovered, and she was naturally glad to see that Xiangling had moved into the garden too. Xiangling said with a smile, "Now that I've come in here I'll have some spare time. If only you would teach me to write poetry, that would be my great good fortune!" Daiyu laughed. "If you want to learn to write poetry, you must take me as your teacher. I'm no master, but I can teach you the general idea." Xiangling smiled. "If you really will, I'll take you as my teacher, and you mustn't get tired of me." Daiyu said, "What is so hard about it that it's even worth learning? It is nothing but opening, developing, turning and closing. <note>original: "起承轉合"; the four movements of a regulated poem.</note> The developing and turning in the middle are two couplets: level tones answer oblique tones, empty words answer full words, and full words answer empty ones. <note>Classical Chinese prosody divides syllables into level and oblique tones, and words into "full" words (nouns and other content words) and "empty" words (particles and function words); the middle couplets of a regulated poem must be parallel in both.</note> But if you really have a remarkable line, it's quite all right even if level and oblique, empty and full, do not match."

Xiangling smiled. "No wonder! I often take an old book of poems and sneak a look at one or two. Some have couplets matched very exactly, and some don't match at all. I've also heard it said, 'The first, third and fifth syllables don't matter; the second, fourth and sixth must be strict.' Yet in the poems of the ancients, some follow the rule and some go wrong on the second, fourth and sixth. So I've been puzzled day after day. Now that I hear you, it turns out these rules don't really matter; the main thing is just that the words and lines should be fresh and original." Daiyu said, "That's exactly the principle. In the end, wording is a secondary matter; the first essential is the conception. If the meaning and feeling are genuine, then even unpolished words will naturally be good. This is called 'not letting the words harm the meaning.'" <note>A phrase from Mencius, warning against reading a poem so literally that the wording obscures its sense.</note>

Xiangling said, "I just love Lu Fangweng's lines, 'The heavy curtains not rolled up, the incense lingers long; the old inkstone, slightly hollowed, gathers ink in plenty.' They are so true and so delightful!" <note>Lu Fangweng is the Song poet Lu You (1125 to 1210).</note> Daiyu said, "You love something shallow and easy like that because you don't understand poetry. Once you fall into that mold, you'll never learn your way out of it. Just listen to me. If you truly want to learn, I have the Complete Works of Wang Mojie here. First take his hundred five-character regulated poems and study them carefully until you know them through and through. Then read a hundred and twenty of Old Du's seven-character regulated poems, and after that one or two hundred of Li Qinglian's seven-character quatrains. <note>Wang Mojie is Wang Wei, Old Du is Du Fu, and Li Qinglian is Li Bai: the three great poets of the Tang dynasty.</note> Once you have these three poets inside you as a foundation, then take a look at Tao Yuanming, Ying, Liu, Xie, Ruan, Yu, Bao and the rest. <note>Earlier poets of the Han to Six Dynasties period, probably Ying Yang, Liu Zhen, Xie Lingyun, Ruan Ji, Yu Xin and Bao Zhao.</note> And clever and quick as you are, in less than a year you're sure to be a master poet!" Xiangling laughed when she heard this. "In that case, my dear miss, please get the book out for me. I'll take it back with me; even reading a few poems at night would be good." At this Daiyu told Zijuan to bring Wang Youcheng's five-character regulated poems and handed them to Xiangling, saying, "Read only the ones marked with red circles; those are all ones I have chosen. Read each one in turn. If there's anything you don't understand, ask your young mistress, or if you see me, I'll explain it to you."

Xiangling took the poems back to the Hengwu Court, set everything else aside, and began reading them one by one under the lamp. Baochai urged her several times to go to bed, but she would not. Seeing her apply herself so painstakingly, Baochai had no choice but to let her be.

One day Daiyu had just finished washing and doing her hair when she saw Xiangling come in all smiles to return the book and ask to exchange it for Du Fu's regulated verse. Daiyu laughed. "How many have you memorized altogether?" Xiangling smiled. "I've read every one that you marked with a red circle." Daiyu said, "And have you grasped anything from them?" Xiangling smiled. "I have grasped a little, but I don't know whether I'm right or not. Let me tell you about it."

<summary>In this page from chapter 48 of Dream of the Red Chamber, Baochai sends medicine for the beaten Jia Lian, and Xiangling asks Lin Daiyu to teach her poetry. Chapter 9, verses 30–31

Śrīdhara's commentary: "If you grant liberation only to your devotees and not to those who are not devotees, then do you too show partiality, born of attachment and aversion?" To this he answers no, with the verse beginning "I am the same." I am the same toward all beings; therefore there is no one dear to me and no one hateful to me. Even so, those who worship me with devotion abide in me, and I too abide in them, as the one who bestows grace on them. The point is this: fire removes the pains of darkness, cold, and the like only for those who tend it, and yet it is not partial; so too the <term>kalpavṛkṣa</term> <gloss>the wish-fulfilling tree of heaven</gloss>. In the same way, though I take the side of my devotees, I have no partiality at all; rather, this is the greatness of devotion to me. ॥ 29 ॥

Madhusūdana's commentary: Moreover, such is the greatness of devotion to me that it produces inequality even in one who is impartial. Hear its greatness:

> Even if a man of very wicked conduct worships me with undivided devotion,
> he must be regarded as righteous, for he has resolved rightly. ॥ 30 ॥

Whoever, even if of very wicked conduct, like Ajāmila and others, worships me with undivided devotion, serving me through some dawning of good fortune, he, though formerly unrighteous, must be regarded as righteous. For he has resolved rightly: he possesses a good and firm determination. <note>Ajāmila is the sinful Brahmin of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa who was saved at death by calling out the name of Nārāyaṇa.</note> ॥ 30 ॥

Śrīdhara's commentary: Moreover, showing that the power of devotion to me lies beyond all reasoning, he speaks the verse beginning "Even if." Even a man of extremely wicked conduct, if he does not practise devotion to some other deity separately, but worships me alone, Śrī Nārāyaṇa, must be regarded as righteous, indeed as excellent. For he has resolved rightly: he has made the fine resolve, "Through worship of the Supreme Lord alone I shall reach my goal." ॥ 30 ॥

Madhusūdana's commentary: Through this very right resolve he abandons his wicked conduct, and

> quickly he becomes righteous of soul and attains lasting peace.
> O son of Kuntī, proclaim it: my devotee never perishes. ॥ 31 ॥

Even one who has long been unrighteous of soul, by the greatness of worshipping me, "quickly," that is, very soon, "becomes righteous of soul," his mind following <term>dharma</term> <gloss>righteousness, sacred duty</gloss>. The meaning is that he casts off his wicked conduct at once and becomes a man of good conduct. Further, he "attains lasting," that is, perpetual, "peace," the ceasing of all longing for the enjoyment of sense objects; he attains it fully, through utter dispassion. Someone might say: "Some devotee of yours, not giving up the wicked conduct he practised before, might fail to become righteous of soul, and so he would surely perish." The Lord answers no to this, speaking as if angered, overcome by his compassion for his devotees: Do not think this a marvel, O son of Kuntī; such, beyond doubt, is the greatness of devotion to me. Therefore, even in front of those who dispute it, make the declaration: make the vow with scorn for them and with pride. My devotee, the devotee of me, <term>Vāsudeva</term> <gloss>Krishna, son of Vasudeva</gloss>, even if of extremely wicked conduct, even if fallen into mortal danger, even if, though rarely fit, he is being entreated, even if utterly deluded and without refuge, does not perish; on the contrary, he attains his goal

This is what he says with "let him make." A "ghee-animal" is something fashioned from ghee; it is called an animal because its form resembles animal flesh. A "flour-animal" is the same. "In attachment" means in extreme desire. Some say that <term>saṅga</term> <gloss>attachment</gloss> means being overpowered by spirits and the like, but that sense is not commonly known; therefore this is the reason. ॥ 37 ॥

(3) **Kullūka.** <term>Saṅga</term> means attachment. If he craves to eat animal flesh, let him make an image of an animal out of ghee or out of flour and eat it; but he should never wish to kill animals without dedicating them to a deity. ॥ 37 ॥

(4) **Rāghavānanda.** A "ghee-animal" is an image of an animal made of ghee. "In attachment" means when there is occasion for an animal offering, or when there is a craving for food from attachment, or for obligatory rites laid down in the <term>smṛti</term> <gloss>traditional law</gloss>; but not in a Vedic rite, since a ghee-animal and the like would conflict with the rule of the eleven <term>avadāna</term> <gloss>portions cut from the victim for the offering</gloss>. That is why it is said, "killing in sacrifice is no killing." ॥ 37 ॥

(5) **Nandana.** He says that one should not commit violence outside the rule, with "let him make." <term>Saṅge</term> means at a gathering, on the occasion of a festival and the like, that is, a meeting of kinsmen and others; on such an occasion let him offer a ghee-animal. In place of the animal let him give plenty of ghee, flour, cakes, and so on. ॥ 37 ॥

(6) **Rāmacandra.** In attachment let him make a ghee-animal; let him make a flour-animal likewise. He should never wish to kill an animal for no purpose. ॥ 37 ॥

### As many hairs as there are on the animal, so many times does he who kills animals for no purpose meet a violent death, after he dies, in birth after birth. ॥ 38 ॥

(1) **Medhātithi.** In that many births, born again and again, he meets a violent death. "He who kills animals for no purpose" is one who slays animals where neither the <term>śruti</term> <gloss>revealed Veda</gloss> nor the <term>smṛti</term> <gloss>traditional law</gloss> enjoins it. From the context, such killing is done for worldly ends, in hunting and the like. The form <term>paśughna</term> <gloss>animal-slayer</gloss> is an archaic Vedic form. ॥ 38 ॥

(2) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa.** <term>Tāvatkṛtvaḥ</term> means that many times. "He who kills animals for no purpose" is the slayer of animals not enjoined by śruti and smṛti. ॥ 38 ॥

(3) **Kullūka.** He who kills animals for his own sake, without dedicating them to a deity, is "one who kills animals for no purpose." When he has died, in as many births as there are hairs on the animal, birth after birth, he meets a violent death. Therefore one should not kill animals for no purpose. In <term>tāvatkṛtvaḥ</term>, the suffix <term>kṛtvasuc</term> is added to a word ending in <term>-vat</term> in the sense of counting the repetitions of an action. <note>This is a point of Pāṇinian grammar: the suffix -kṛtvas forms adverbs meaning "so many times."</note> Here the word <term>ha</term> <gloss>indeed</gloss> serves to indicate that the matter is well known from scripture. ॥ 38 ॥

(4) **Rāghavānanda.** He states the penalty for the opposite course with "as many." Here the word <term>ha</term> signals a well-known matter. ॥ 38 ॥

(5) **Nandana.** <term>Tāvatkṛtvaḥ</term> means that many times. The word <term>ha</term> expresses compassion. ॥ 38 ॥

(6) **Rāmacandra.** The man who kills animals for no purpose, having done killing in this world through unrighteousness, after death attains a condition like that of an animal as many times as the animal has hairs, eight crores of hairs, in birth after birth. <note>A crore is ten million; "eight crores" is a conventional figure for the number of hairs on a body.</note> ॥ 38 ॥

### The Self-existent himself created animals for the sake of sacrifice; sacrifice is for the prosperity of this whole world; therefore killing in sacrifice is no killing. ॥ 39 ॥

(1) **Medhātithi.** The fault just described does not apply here. This is said precisely to remove that fault in the case of killing that is enjoined by śruti and smṛti and forms part of a sacrifice. Animals were created, that is, brought forth, by the Self-existent, that is, by <term>Prajāpati</term> <gloss>the Lord of Creatures</gloss>. "Himself" is an <term>arthavāda</term> <gloss>a commendatory statement, not a rule</gloss>. The sacrifice, such as the <term>Jyotiṣṭoma</term> <gloss>a Soma sacrifice</gloss>, is for the prosperity of this world, of all; prosperity means power, nourishment, abundance. Therefore whatever killing takes place in it is to be understood as no killing. It is said this way because the sin born of injury is removed. ॥ 39 ॥

(2) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa.** Here he removes the doubt, "How can killing for sacrifice be free of such a fault?", with "for the sake of sacrifice." "For the prosperity of the world" means for its coming into being: through the oblation the sun is nourished, then comes rain, then seed, and in this chain semen arises and living beings are produced. By this it is stated that there is no such fault, since by the killing of one animal many living beings are brought forth. ॥ 39 ॥

VALĀHAKAVAGGA <note>The Chapter on Rain-Clouds</note>. 103

102.

1. "There are, monks, these four kinds of rain-cloud <note>original: "valāhakā"</note>. Which four?
The one that thunders but does not rain . . . and so on . . . the one that both thunders and rains. <note>The Pali "pe" is an abbreviation mark, standing for repeated material the editor has left out; here the full list was given in the preceding discourse.</note>
These, monks, are the four kinds of rain-cloud.

2. "In just the same way, monks, there are these four kinds of persons like rain-clouds
to be found existing in the world. Which four?
The one who thunders but does not rain . . . and so on . . . the one who both thunders and rains.

3. "And how, monks, is a person one who thunders but does not rain?
Here, monks, a certain person masters the teaching <note>original: "dhammam pariyāpuṇāti", literally "learns the Dhamma thoroughly", that is, by heart</note>:
the discourses, the mixed prose and verse, the expositions, the verses, the inspired utterances, the sayings "thus it was said",
the birth stories, the marvels, and the question-and-answer catechisms. <note>These are the nine traditional "limbs" of the Buddha's teaching: <term>sutta</term>, <term>geyya</term>, <term>veyyākaraṇa</term>, <term>gāthā</term>, <term>udāna</term>, <term>itivuttaka</term>, <term>jātaka</term>, <term>abbhutadhamma</term> and <term>vedalla</term>.</note> Yet he does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering"
. . . and so on . . . he does not understand as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." <note>The abbreviation stands for the full formula of the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path to its cessation.</note>
In this way, monks, a person is one who thunders but does not rain. Just as,
monks, that rain-cloud thunders but does not rain, of such a kind,
monks, do I declare this person to be.

4. "And how, monks, is a person one who rains but does not thunder?
Here, monks, a certain person does not master the teaching:
the discourses . . . and so on . . . the question-and-answer catechisms. Yet he understands as it really is: "This is
suffering" . . . and so on . . . he understands as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way,
monks, a person is one who rains but does not thunder. Just as
that, monks, . . . do I declare.

5. "And how, monks, is a person one who neither thunders nor
rains?
Here, monks, a certain person does not master the teaching:
the discourses . . . the question-and-answer catechisms. Nor does he understand as it really
is: "This is suffering" . . . he does not understand as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks,
a person is one who neither thunders nor rains. Just as that,
monks, . . . do I declare.

6. "And how, monks, is a person one who both thunders and rains?
Here, monks, a certain person masters the teaching:
the discourses . . . the question-and-answer catechisms. And he understands as it really is: "This is suffering"
. . . he understands as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, a person both thunders
and rains. Just as, monks, that rain-cloud
both thunders and rains, of such a kind, monks, do I declare this
person to be."

<summary>This page gives the Buddha's discourse on four kinds of rain-cloud (Aṅguttara Nikāya, Fours, no. 102). It compares people to clouds: some learn the scriptures by heart but lack insight into the Four Noble Truths (thunder without rain), some have insight without learning, some have neither, and some have both.</summary>

**Root text** <note>original: "mū°", short for <term>mūla</term> <gloss>the root verses of Svātmārāma, as distinct from the commentary</gloss></note> . . . and strength of body arises, free from every affliction.
By this method, truly, he becomes a lord among yogis on the face of the earth. ॥ 56 ॥

### Now the Śītalī ॥ <note><term>Śītalī</term> <gloss>"the cooling one"</gloss>, a breath-retention practised by drawing air in over the tongue.</note>

Drawing in the air with the tongue, let the wise one perform the breath-retention as before,
and then slowly expel the breath through the two nostrils. ॥ 57 ॥

Abdominal swellings, disorders of the spleen and other diseases, fever, bile, hunger and thirst,
and poisons: this breath-retention called Śītalī destroys them all. ॥ 58 ॥

---

->॥ Commentary ॥<- <note>This is the Sanskrit commentary printed with the root text, generally identified as Brahmānanda's <term>Jyotsnā</term> <gloss>"Moonlight"</gloss>.</note>

"Bhavet" ॥ Strength <note>original: "sattvam", glossed as "balam", strength</note> of the body <note>"dehasya" glossed as "śarīrasya"</note> also arises. By this method just stated, that is, the method of practice, the lord of yogis, meaning one who is like Indra among yogis, becomes truly free from all afflictions on the face of the earth. Following the maxim "every statement carries an emphasis" <note>original: "sarvaṃ vākyaṃ sāvadhāraṇam"</note>, the meaning is that the fruit which has been stated is indeed true. ॥ 56 ॥

He now describes the Śītalī breath-retention ॥ "Jihvayā" <note>"with the tongue"</note>. With the tongue put out beyond the lips, shaped like the lower half of a bird's beak, drawing in the air: the meaning is "having slowly made the inhalation" <note><term>pūraka</term> <gloss>the in-breath</gloss></note>. "As before" means as in the Sūryabhedana: the words "having carried out the performance of the retention" <note><term>kumbha</term>, that is <term>kumbhaka</term> <gloss>holding of the breath</gloss></note> are to be supplied. "The wise one": one whose understanding is excellent. Through the two openings of the nose, that is, through the cavities of the nostrils, "śanakaiḥ", meaning simply "slowly". <note>The commentator explains the grammar: by Pāṇini's rule beginning "avyaya-sarvanāmnām", the suffix <term>akac</term> is inserted into the adverb "śanaiḥ", giving the form "śanakaiḥ" with the same meaning.</note> Let him expel <note><term>recaka</term> <gloss>the out-breath</gloss></note> the breath, that is, the air. ॥ 57 ॥

He states the benefits of the Śītalī ॥ "Gulma". Gulma and plīha, abdominal swelling and disease of the spleen, are particular diseases; those disorders which begin with these two are "gulma, plīha and the rest". Fever: the disease called fever. Bile: disorders of the bile. Hunger: the desire to eat. Thirst: the desire to drink water. Poisons: the disorders produced by the venom of snakes and the like. "Called Śītalī" <note>original: "śītalī-nāma"</note>: here "nāma" is an indeclinable carrying the sense "well known as". This breath-retention just described "nihanti", destroys, that is, destroys utterly. The word "kumbha" in the femin- <note>The sentence breaks off at the foot of the page; the commentator is explaining why the feminine form "kumbhikā" is used.</note>

---

->॥ Vernacular explanation ॥<- <note>original: "bhāṣā", a paraphrase in the Hindi of the period, printed beneath the Sanskrit commentary</note>

"Bhavet" ॥ Strength comes to the body, and by this method of practice that has been described, one who is like Indra among yogis becomes free from all afflictions on the earth. The fruit that has been stated here is true. ॥ 56 ॥

Now we describe the fourth, the Śītalī breath-retention ॥ "Jihvayā". Putting one's tongue out beyond the lips like the lower half of a bird's beak, drawing in the air and making the inhalation, one should then carry out the breath-retention just as was described earlier for the Sūryabhedana. Then he whose understanding is fine should slowly, slowly expel the air through the openings of the nose. ॥ 57 ॥

We describe the benefits of the Śītalī ॥ "Gulma". Abdominal swelling and disease of the spleen, and the diseases that begin with these; and fever, and disorders of the bile; and the desire to eat, the desire to drink water; and the venom of snakebite and other poisons as well: all these the breath-retention named Śītalī removes. ॥ 58 ॥

<summary>This page of the Haṭhayogapradīpikā (verses 2.56 to 2.58) closes the account of the Sītkārī breath-retention and teaches the Śītalī, in which air is drawn in over a protruding tongue, held, and released through the nose. It lists the ailments Śītalī is said to cure, with a Sanskrit commentary and a Hindi paraphrase explaining each word.</summary>

the Supreme <note>original: "paraḥ"; the OCR's following word "anakān" is unclear and probably corrupt</note> is the Great Lord, all-knowing, the maker <note>original: "sakala-jagan-mātṛ", literally "the measurer" or "mother" of the whole world</note> and ordainer of the whole world. How is he to be known? By inference, or by <unclear>śramāt</unclear> <note>the reading "śramāt", "by toil", looks corrupt; "āgamāt", "by scripture", would be expected alongside inference</note>. For it is like this. The inference runs: "The perceived world under dispute has a cause, because it comes to be after not having been <note>the OCR reads "babhūtvā"; the sense requires "abhūtvā bhāvitvāt", "because of coming into being after not being"</note>, like a painting." After that, what has been understood in general through inference is known in its particulars through yoga. The other, the individual soul <note><term>jīva</term> <gloss>the embodied self</gloss></note>, is established simply by one's own experience. Nature <note><term>prakṛti</term> <gloss>primal matter, the unconscious source of the world</gloss></note> becomes active so that the difference between these two, the higher and the lower, may be known. Its acting for the sake of another will be explained later. And as to its acting for its own sake: towards whichever conscious being <note><term>puruṣa</term> <gloss>the spirit or witness</gloss></note> it has displayed itself through discrimination, towards him it ceases to act <note>original: "udāste", literally "sits apart, becomes indifferent"</note>. How can unconscious nature become active? Activity is observed even in unconscious things, such as milk, for the sake of a result such as the nourishment of a calf <note>the classic Sāṃkhya example: milk flows of itself to feed the calf</note>. ॥ 1 ॥

Next, to the question "Who are qualified for liberation?", he says:

Sūtra: Of the one who is free from passion, because for him it is accomplished. ॥ 2 ॥ <note>original: "viraktasya tatsiddheḥ"</note>

And so scripture says: "Having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth and the desire for worlds, they then go about living as mendicants," and: "Having become calm, controlled, withdrawn, patient and collected, he sees the Self within the Self alone." <note>Both quotations come from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.</note> ॥ 2 ॥

If liberation follows upon hearing the teaching, because of dispassion, then everyone would be liberated after receiving a teacher's instruction; and that is not what we see. To this he says:

Sūtra: It is not accomplished by hearing alone, because of the strength of beginningless latent impressions. ॥ 3 ॥ <note>original: "na śravaṇamātrāt tatsiddhir anādivāsanāyā balavattvāt"; <term>vāsanā</term> <gloss>the residual impressions left by past actions and experiences</gloss></note>

Liberation does not follow straight after hearing; rather, because of the strength of the beginningless latent impressions, liberation is swift in one case and comes only after a long time in another. <note>The commentary is very compressed here: the force of the latent impressions decides whether liberation comes quickly or slowly.</note> ॥ 3 ॥

He gives a further reason:

Sūtra: Or, as with one who has many servants, for each one separately. ॥ 4 ॥ <note>The OCR reads "bahubhṛtvavahā pratyekam", which appears to be a corruption of "bahubhṛtyavad vā pratyekam"; it is translated in that sense. The point of the image is explained on the next page.</note>

<summary>This page of a Sāṃkhya commentary describes the Supreme Lord, known by inference and by yoga, and the individual soul, known by experience, and says that nature acts so that the two may be told apart. It then comments on three sūtras: liberation belongs to the dispassionate, it does not come from hearing the teaching alone because of the strength of beginningless latent impressions, and a further reason is introduced through the image of a master with many servants.</summary>
